slides.heading: Client Rights & Abuse Prevention
bullets: The rights of every person we serve
Practices that are never allowed
Types and signs of abuse and neglect
How to respond, report and protect the client
slides.narration: Welcome to Client Rights and Abuse Prevention. Every person we serve at Spectrum Squad has rights, and every one of us has a part in protecting them. You will learn what those rights look like in a real session, at home, at school, in the community, or at our clinic. We will cover practices that are never allowed, and the emergency procedures you may only use when you are trained and authorized. You will learn the types and signs of abuse and neglect, including abuse by staff. Finally, we will walk through how to respond, how to report, how to keep the client safe afterward, and how our grievance process works. Let's get started.

slides.heading: Dignity, Respect and Freedom From Harm
bullets: Treat every client with dignity and respect
Freedom from abuse, neglect and exploitation
Speak to and about clients respectfully
Respect each family's culture, language and values
slides.narration: Every client has the right to be treated with dignity and respect. That means talking to a client the way you would want someone to talk to you, even when the client does not use words. Never joke at a client's expense. Every client also has the right to be free from abuse, neglect and exploitation. Respect includes culture, too. Families have different languages, beliefs and ways of raising children. Ask what matters to them, and work with your B C B A so that goals and teaching fit the family's values, instead of expecting the family to fit us.

slides.heading: The Right to Privacy
bullets: Protect client information and records
Give privacy during toileting and dressing
Never discuss clients in public or online
No photos or videos without approval and consent
slides.narration: Clients have a right to privacy. That covers their health information, their records, and their bodies. During toileting or dressing programs, give as much privacy as is safe, and follow the plan your B C B A wrote. Never discuss clients in public places, and never post about a client on social media, even without a name. Do not take photos or videos of a client unless Spectrum Squad's policy allows it and the guardian has given consent. Imagine a staff member at your client's school asks you what the child's diagnosis is. Even if they seem helpful, do not share it. Politely say you are not able to discuss it, and let your supervisor know. Privacy is also protected by federal law.

slides.heading: Consent, Assent and Participation
bullets: Clients and families help shape the treatment plan
Guardians give consent for minors
Assent is the client's willingness, moment to moment
Honor withdrawal of assent and tell your B C B A
slides.narration: Clients have the right to take part in decisions about their own treatment. For children, and for adults who have a legal guardian, the parent or guardian gives informed consent to the treatment plan. Assent is different. It is the client's own willingness to take part, shown moment to moment through words, body language and behavior. A child who comes to the table smiling is showing assent. A child who turns away, pushes materials off the table, cries, or says stop may be withdrawing assent. When that happens, never use physical force to make them keep going. Pause, give space, offer a break or choices, and follow the assent guidelines your B C B A has written. Then let your B C B A know, so the program can be adjusted to work better for the client.

slides.heading: Least Restrictive Care and Refusal
bullets: Use the least restrictive effective intervention
Start with reinforcement and teaching skills
Clients and families may refuse or stop services
Respect refusal and tell your B C B A that day
slides.narration: Clients have the right to the least restrictive effective intervention. We always start with the gentlest strategy that works, like reinforcement, teaching new skills, and changing the environment, before anything more intrusive. Any more restrictive procedure must be written into the behavior plan by the B C B A and agreed to by the guardian. As an R B T, you never invent a new consequence on your own. Clients and families also have the right to refuse services, to stop a program, or to end services completely. Say a parent tells you she no longer wants you working on a certain goal. Do not argue. Thank her, write down what she said accurately, and tell your B C B A that same day. A family should never be threatened or treated worse because they said no.

slides.heading: Practices That Are Never Allowed
bullets: No hitting, spanking or any corporal punishment
No seclusion and no unapproved restraint
No withholding food, water or bathroom access
No humiliation, threats, yelling or name-calling
slides.narration: Some practices are never allowed at Spectrum Squad, no matter who asks. Never use corporal punishment. That means no hitting, spanking, slapping, pinching, or causing pain of any kind. Never use seclusion, which means leaving a client alone in a room or space they cannot leave. Never use a restraint that is not approved in the client's plan, or one you are not trained to use. Never take away food, water, or bathroom access as a consequence for behavior. And never humiliate a client. That includes yelling, threats, name-calling, or mocking. If a parent or teacher asks you to use one of these practices, politely explain that you cannot, and tell your B C B A. Their request does not make it okay.

slides.heading: Emergency and Crisis Procedures
bullets: Only use procedures you're trained and authorized for
They must be written in the client's behavior plan
Use only to prevent serious harm, then stop
Tell your B C B A and document every use
slides.narration: Sometimes a client's behavior puts people in real danger. You may only use an emergency or crisis procedure when three things are true. It is written in that client's behavior plan, you have been trained on it, and you are authorized to use it. Even then, it is only used to prevent serious harm. It is never a punishment, and never used for convenience. It ends as soon as the danger is over. For example, if a client suddenly runs toward a busy parking lot outside the clinic, you follow the safety steps in the plan. Afterward, tell your B C B A right away and document what happened, what you did, and how long it lasted, following Spectrum Squad's policy. If you are not trained on a procedure, do not try it. Keep everyone safe, get help, and call emergency services if needed.

slides.heading: Types of Abuse and Neglect
bullets: Physical, sexual and emotional abuse
Neglect: not meeting basic needs or safety
Exploitation of money, property or the person
Can happen anywhere, including by staff
slides.narration: Abuse and neglect can take several forms. Physical abuse is causing injury or pain on purpose. Sexual abuse is any sexual contact or behavior with a client, or exposing them to sexual material. Emotional abuse includes constant threats, insults, or frightening someone. Neglect is failing to give a person what they need to be safe and healthy, like food, clean clothes, medical care, supervision, or a safe place to live. Exploitation is using a client, or their money, property, or benefits, for someone else's gain. Watch for this especially with adult clients. Abuse can happen anywhere, and can come from family members, other children, teachers, and sometimes from staff. Being a coworker never protects someone from being reported.

slides.heading: Signs to Watch For
bullets: Injuries that don't match the explanation
Sudden changes in behavior, sleep or eating
New fear of a certain person, place or touch
Our clients may not be able to tell you
slides.narration: Watch for signs that something may be wrong. Physical signs include bruises or marks that do not match the explanation, or injuries in places that are hard to hurt by accident. Neglect may look like ongoing hunger, poor hygiene, or untreated medical needs. Behavior changes matter too. A sudden jump in self-injury or aggression, a new fear of a certain person, place, or type of touch, trouble sleeping, or losing skills they had already learned can all be warning signs. Not every change means abuse, but every real concern deserves to be shared. Many of our clients with autism have limited speech, or may not understand that what is happening to them is wrong. They may not be able to tell you. That means we have to watch even more closely. Trust what you notice, and speak up.

slides.heading: How to Respond and Report
bullets: Stay calm, listen, and keep the client safe
Don't investigate or ask leading questions
Tell your supervisor immediately
Report to child welfare or police when required
slides.narration: If a client tells you something, or you see something that worries you, stay calm. Listen. Do not ask leading questions, do not promise to keep it a secret, and do not try to investigate on your own. If anyone is in immediate danger, call emergency services first. Then tell your supervisor immediately, the same day, not at the end of the week. Telling your supervisor is required, but it may not be enough by itself. Under Nevada law, many people who work with children are mandatory reporters, and they must report directly to the child welfare agency or to law enforcement. Telling your supervisor does not replace that personal duty. For adult clients, concerns may need to go to adult protective services or law enforcement. The separate Mandatory Reporter course explains who must report in Nevada, where, and how quickly. Write down what you saw and heard, using exact words.

slides.heading: Protect the Client, Never Retaliate
bullets: Client safety comes first after any concern
Don't warn anyone who may be involved
Share only with people who need to know
Never retaliate against anyone who reports
slides.narration: After a concern is raised, the client's safety comes first. If a staff member may be involved, Spectrum Squad may remove that person from the client's case while the concern is looked into. Do not warn the person who may be involved, and do not talk about the report with coworkers or the family unless your supervisor or the investigators ask you to. Retaliation is never allowed. That means no one may punish, threaten, ignore, or treat differently a client, a family, or a coworker because they reported a concern or made a complaint. An R B T who reports a teammate should never be given worse hours or left out. If you see retaliation happening, report that too.

slides.heading: Filing a Grievance
bullets: Clients and families can file a complaint anytime
Listen, and help them reach your supervisor
Follow Spectrum Squad's grievance policy
No retaliation, ever, for speaking up
slides.narration: Clients and families have the right to file a grievance, which is a formal complaint, without fear of retaliation. Sometimes the complaint will be about you. If a family brings a complaint to you, listen without getting defensive, and do not try to talk them out of it. Let them know they have the right to make a complaint, and help them reach your supervisor or the office, following Spectrum Squad's grievance policy. Then tell your supervisor about the conversation. The family's services should not be cut or changed because they complained. Staff can raise concerns too. If your supervisor is part of the problem, go to clinical leadership or the office.

slides.heading: Recap and Next Steps
bullets: Protect dignity, privacy, consent and assent
Never use prohibited practices
Watch closely, report right away, protect the client
Take the quiz: you need 80% to pass
slides.narration: Let's recap. Every client has the right to dignity, respect, privacy, and freedom from abuse, neglect and exploitation. They have the right to take part in their treatment, to give or withdraw assent, to the least restrictive effective care, to refuse services, and to file a grievance without retaliation. Corporal punishment, seclusion, unapproved restraint, withholding food, water or the bathroom, and humiliation are never allowed. Only use crisis procedures that are in the plan and that you are trained and authorized to use. Know the signs of abuse and neglect, and remember that our clients may not be able to tell you. If you have a concern, tell your supervisor immediately, and report to the proper agency when the law requires it. Thank you for the care you bring to this work. Now it's time to take the quiz. You need eighty percent to pass.

quiz.question: During table work, a seven-year-old client pushes the materials away, starts crying and says "stop." What should the R B T do?
choices: Physically guide the child's hands to finish the task
Pause, offer a break or choices, follow the assent guidelines, and tell the B C B A
Remove the child's favorite toy until they go back to work
Ignore the crying and keep presenting the task at the same pace
quiz.explanation: Pushing away, crying and saying stop can signal withdrawal of assent. Never force participation; pause, follow the assent guidelines and let your B C B A know so the program can be adjusted.

quiz.question: During an in-home session, a parent tells you, "When he hits, don't give him his lunch until he calms down." What should you do?
choices: Do it, because the parent has given permission
Do it once to see whether it works
Ask another R B T on the case what they would do
Politely explain you can't withhold food as a consequence, and tell your B C B A
quiz.explanation: Withholding food, water or bathroom access as a consequence is never allowed, even if a parent asks. Decline politely and tell your B C B A.

quiz.question: A client runs toward a busy parking lot outside the clinic. Their behavior plan includes a safety procedure you are trained and authorized to use. What is correct?
choices: Use the procedure in the plan, stop when the danger is over, then tell your B C B A and document it
Use the procedure for the rest of the session so the client learns a lesson
Use a hold you saw in a video because it looks safer
Put the client alone in an empty room until they calm down
quiz.explanation: Crisis procedures are only for preventing serious harm, must follow the plan, and end when the danger is over. Every use is reported to your B C B A and documented.

quiz.question: A friendly staff member at your client's school asks you what the child's diagnosis is. What should you do?
choices: Tell them, since they work with the child too
Tell them only the diagnosis but not the treatment details
Politely say you can't discuss it, and let your supervisor know
Show them the child's treatment plan on your phone
quiz.explanation: Client information is private. Politely decline to share it and let your supervisor know about the request.

quiz.question: Your client, who has very limited speech, has new bruises on both upper arms and flinches and hides when a certain adult comes into the room. What should you do?
choices: Wait a few weeks to see if more bruises appear before saying anything
Tell your supervisor immediately and follow mandatory reporting requirements
Ask the child a series of yes-or-no questions about who hurt them
Ask the adult directly how the bruises happened
quiz.explanation: Unexplained injuries and new fear of a person are warning signs, and our clients may not be able to tell you. Report right away and do not investigate yourself.

quiz.question: An R B T reports a suspected abuse concern about a child to her supervisor. Which statement is true?
choices: Telling the supervisor may not be enough; mandatory reporters must also report to child welfare or law enforcement
Once the supervisor knows, the R B T has no further responsibility
The R B T should wait for the supervisor's permission before any report is made
Reports only need to be made if the R B T is completely sure abuse happened
quiz.explanation: Telling your supervisor does not replace a personal mandatory reporting duty to the child welfare agency or law enforcement. The Mandatory Reporter course covers the Nevada details.

quiz.question: At a community outing, you see a coworker grab a child roughly by the arm and yell insults at him. What is the best response?
choices: Say nothing, since the coworker is senior to you
Talk to the coworker privately and warn them a report may be coming
Post about it in the team group chat so others can watch the coworker
Make sure the child is safe, tell your supervisor immediately, and report to the agency if required
quiz.explanation: Abuse can come from staff, and being a coworker never protects someone from being reported. Do not warn the person involved, and share only with people who need to know.

quiz.question: After an R B T reports a safety concern about a teammate, her hours are cut and the team starts leaving her out. What is this?
choices: A normal scheduling change that has nothing to do with the report
A fair consequence for causing problems on the team
Retaliation, which is never allowed and should be reported
Acceptable as long as no one says it is because of the report
quiz.explanation: No one may be punished, ignored or treated differently for reporting a concern. If you see retaliation, report that too.

quiz.question: A parent tells you she no longer wants you working on one of her son's goals. What should you do?
choices: Respect her decision, write down what she said, and tell your B C B A that same day
Explain why she is wrong and keep working on the goal
Keep working on the goal when she is not in the room
Tell her services will have to end if she won't follow the plan
quiz.explanation: Clients and families have the right to refuse or stop services. Respect the decision, document it accurately and let your B C B A know so the team can follow up.

quiz.question: A family tells you they are unhappy with how a staff member treated their daughter and want to complain. What should you do?
choices: Try to talk them out of it so the staff member doesn't get in trouble
Tell them complaints may affect their schedule
Tell them to handle it themselves and change the subject
Listen, let them know they have the right to complain, help them reach your supervisor or the office, and tell your supervisor
quiz.explanation: Clients and families have the right to file a grievance without retaliation. Listen without getting defensive, help them use Spectrum Squad's grievance process, and tell your supervisor.
